holidays.name: National Paperclip Day
holidays.description: Salute the humble bent wire that holds the paper world together. Today is the day to appreciate the tiny loop of metal that has rescued countless documents from chaos. Bonus points for making a paperclip chain, a hook, or an emergency phone-SIM ejector.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It honors the paperclip, whose looped-wire design became a staple of offices around the turn of the 20th century.
holidays.funFact: During World War II, Norwegians wore paperclips on their lapels as a quiet symbol of unity and resistance against occupation, because the clip 'binds together.'

holidays.name: National Snail Day
holidays.description: A day to slow down and celebrate the world's most laid-back commuters. Snails carry their homes on their backs and leave shimmering trails wherever they go. Take a gentle garden stroll, and maybe skip the escargot.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin, created to shine a spotlight on these slow-moving mollusks.
holidays.funFact: A garden snail's tongue, called a radula, can hold thousands of microscopic teeth, which it uses to scrape up its food.

holidays.name: Mount Everest Day
holidays.description: A day to look up, way up, at the tallest mountain on Earth. It celebrates the moment humans first stood on the roof of the world, and honors the climbers and Sherpa guides who still take on its icy slopes.
holidays.origin: It marks the anniversary of May 29, 1953, when Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay of Nepal became the first confirmed climbers to reach the summit of Everest.
holidays.funFact: Everest grows slightly taller over time because the tectonic plates pushing the Himalayas upward are still colliding.
